claims.claim: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury.
claims.source: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury, whereas in mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss (Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Brignull et al., 2009; Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Cruz et al., 2015; Ryals and Rubel, 1988).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss.
claims.source: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury, whereas in mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss (Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Brignull et al., 2009; Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Cruz et al., 2015; Ryals and Rubel, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established research.

claims.claim: The zebrafish lateral line system is a powerful in vivo model to study the cellular and molecular basis of hair cell regeneration.
claims.source: We and others showed that the zebrafish lateral line system is a powerful in vivo model to study the cellular and molecular basis of hair cell regeneration (Kniss et al., 2016; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma and Raible, 2009; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Viader-Llargués et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work by the authors and others.

claims.claim: Lateral line organs (neuromasts) contain approximately 60 cells, composed of central sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells and an outer ring of mantle cells.
claims.source: The lateral line organs (neuromasts), distributed on the head and along the body contain approximately 60 cells, composed of central sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells and an outer ring of mantle cells (Figure 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the description in the text and the schematic shown in Figure 1A-B.

claims.claim: The morphology and function of sensory hair cells are evolutionarily conserved from fish to mammals.
claims.source: Importantly, the morphology and function of sensory hair cells are evolutionarily conserved from fish to mammals (Duncan and Fritzsch, 2012; Nicolson, 2005; Whitfield, 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Mutations in genes causing deafness in humans also disrupt hair cells in the zebrafish lateral line.
claims.source: For example, mutations in genes causing deafness in humans also disrupt hair cells in the zebrafish lateral line (Nicolson, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration in zebrafish.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, our findings that Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration is also true in the mouse cochlea (Li et al., 2015b; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own research.

claims.claim: Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration in the mouse cochlea.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, our findings that Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration is also true in the mouse cochlea (Li et al., 2015b; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation.
claims.source: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation, and in chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells (Balak et al., 1990; Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Harris et al., 2003; Jones and Corwin, 1996; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma et al., 2008; Wibowo et al., 2011; Williams and Holder, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells.
claims.source: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation, and in chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells (Balak et al., 1990; Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Harris et al., 2003; Jones and Corwin, 1996; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma et al., 2008; Wibowo et al., 2011; Williams and Holder, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There are two major support cell lineages: support cells that divide symmetrically to form two progenitor cells (amplifying divisions) and support cells that divide to form two hair cells (differentiating divisions).
claims.source: Using time-lapse analyses and tracking of all dividing cells in regenerating neuromasts, coupled with cell fate analyses, we previously identified two major support cell lineages: 1) support cells that divide symmetrically to form two progenitor cells (amplifying divisions); and 2) support cells that divide to form two hair cells (differentiating divisions) (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Amplifying divisions occur in the dorsal-ventral (D/V) poles and differentiating divisions occur in the center.
claims.source: The two cell behaviors display a striking spatial compartmentalization. Amplifying divisions occur in the dorsal-ventral (D/V) poles and differentiating divisions occur in the center.
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior experimental observations cited in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Mantle cells surrounding the support cells only divide after severe injury to the neuromasts but rarely divide if only hair cells are killed.
claims.source: Mantle cells surrounding the support cells only divide after severe injury to the neuromasts but rarely divide if only hair cells are killed.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior experimental observations by the authors.

claims.claim: There are at least four support cell types in a neuromast that likely play different functions in balancing progenitor maintenance with differentiation.
claims.source: Thus, there are at least four support cell types in a neuromast that likely play different functions in balancing progenitor maintenance with differentiation to ensure the life-long ability to regenerate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed cell behaviors and the scRNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: Unsupervised clustering partitioned 1521 neuromast cells into 14 different clusters.
claims.source: Unsupervised clustering partitioned 1521 neuromast cells into 14 different clusters (Butler et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a direct result from the scRNA-Seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Seven major neuromast cell types were identified from the 14 clusters.
claims.source: We combined some of the less well-defined clusters and identified seven major neuromast cell types (Figure 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is based on the scRNA-Seq analysis and shown in Figure 1C-D.

claims.claim: Cluster 1 represents differentiated hair cells.
claims.source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Cluster 2 represents young hair cells.
claims.source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Cluster 4 represents proliferating hair cell progenitors.
claims.source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Clusters 3 and 10 represent amplifying support cells.
claims.source: The other cycling cells belong to clusters 3 and 10, and because they fail to express hair cell lineage genes, they likely represent amplifying support cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Mature, differentiated hair cells are centrally and apically located in a neuromast.
claims.source: Mature, differentiated hair cells are centrally and apically located in a neuromast (tekt3, Figure 1F,R,S; dark green).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1F, R, S.

claims.claim: Young hair cells form a ring immediately above the mature hair cells and express atoh1b.
claims.source: Immediately above the mature hair cells are young hair cells that form a ring and express atoh1b (cluster 2, Figure 1G,R,S).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G, R, S.

claims.claim: Delta ligands are only expressed in a subset of the young hair cells.
claims.source: Figure 1H shows that delta ligands are only expressed in a subset of the young hair cells (light green).
claims.evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: lfng and ebf3a mark the most basal, central support cells.
claims.source: lfng and ebf3a mark the most basal, central support cells (Figure 1I,J,S,U; blue).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I, J, S, U.

claims.claim: lfng is expressed in support cells that are situated underneath hair cells in the mouse cochlea.
claims.source: lfng is also expressed in support cells that are situated underneath hair cells in the mouse cochlea (Maass et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The central cell population in neuromasts expresses gata2a/b and slc1a3a/glasta, which are markers for hematopoietic and neural stem cells, respectively.
claims.source: The central cell population in neuromasts expresses gata2a/b and slc1a3a/glasta, which are markers for hematopoietic and neural stem cells, respectively (Figure 3I; Supplementary file 6, Hewitt et al., 2016; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and citations to prior research on these markers in other systems.

claims.claim: A subset of central cells expresses stem cell-associated genes such as isl1 and fabp7a.
claims.source: Within the central cell cluster, a subset of cells expresses other stem cell-associated genes, such as isl1 and fabp7a (clusters 7, 9; Figure 1K; Kim et al., 2016; Makarev and Gorivodsky, 2014; Morihiro et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1K and citations to prior research on these genes as stem cell markers.

claims.claim: Members of the retinoic acid pathway, such as crabp2a, dhrs3a and rdh10a are restricted to clusters 7 and 9.
claims.source: In addition, members of the retinoic acid pathway, such as crabp2a, dhrs3a and rdh10a are restricted to clusters 7 and 9 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Central cells only give rise to hair cells and do not self-renew.
claims.source: Even though central cells express genes characteristic for stem cells in other systems, our lineage tracing experiments showed that they only give rise to hair cells and do not self-renew (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior lineage tracing experiments by the authors.

claims.claim: Cells in the D/V poles of neuromasts that express wnt2 are located immediately adjacent to the mantle cells and proliferate to generate more support cells that do not differentiate into hair cells.
claims.source: Cells in the D/V poles of neuromasts that express wnt2 are located immediately adjacent to the mantle cells and proliferate to generate more support cells that do not differentiate into hair cells (see below; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior experimental data cited from the authors' work.

claims.claim: Mantle cells are the outermost cells in a neuromast and are marked by ovgp1 and sfrp1a.
claims.source: The most distinct support cell population are the mantle cells represented in clusters 5 and 6 and marked by ovgp1 and sfrp1a (Figure 1M–N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1M-N.

claims.claim: Lineage tracing of mantle cells in medaka revealed that mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells and constitute long term stem cells.
claims.source: Lineage tracing of mantle cells in medaka revealed that mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research in medaka.

claims.claim: Mantle cells give rise to postembryonic neuromasts during development and restore neuromasts on regenerating tail tips.
claims.source: In addition, they give rise to postembryonic neuromasts during development and restore neuromasts on regenerating tail tips (Dufourcq et al., 2006; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007; Jones and Corwin, 1993; Ledent, 2002; Wada et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Genes such as fndc7rs4, tfap2a, tcf7l2, hopx, cmah and alpl are expressed in a ring-like pattern in mantle cells, anterior-posterior (A/P) cells and polar cells.
claims.source: We also identified a number of genes that are expressed in a ring-like pattern, such as fndc7rs4, tfap2a, tcf7l2, hopx, cmah and alpl (Figure 1O, data not shown). These genes are not restricted to any cluster but are expressed in mantle cells, anterior-posterior (A/P) cells and polar cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1O.

claims.claim: hopx, cmah and alpl are stem cell markers in different systems.
claims.source: Interestingly, hopx, cmah and alpl are stem cell markers in different systems raising the possibility that they also mark stem cells in neuromasts (Fuchs, 2009; Takeda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on these genes as stem cell markers.

claims.claim: Cells in clusters 10, 3 and 4 express pcna (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) and stmn1a.
claims.source: Cells in clusters 10, 3 and 4 express pcna (proliferating cell nuclear antigen), required for DNA replication and repair, as well as the mitotic spindle regulator stmn1a (Figures 1D, 2A and D; Supplementary file 4; Rubin and Atweh, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 1D, 2A and D, and a citation to prior research on these genes.

claims.claim: Genes that regulate early versus later phases of the cell cycle are expressed in complementary subsets of the pcna+ cells.
claims.source: Genes that regulate early versus later phases of the cell cycle are expressed in complementary subsets of the pcna +cells (Figure 2B,C, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: Genes with GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4, are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14.
claims.source: Genes with the associated GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4 are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14, whereas genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot (cdk1; Figure 2B,C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 2B, C, D.

claims.claim: Genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot.
claims.source: Genes with the associated GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4 are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14, whereas genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot (cdk1; Figure 2B,C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 2B, C, D.

claims.claim: Cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells.
claims.source: Thus, cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells (Figure 2E–G; support cells, red), whereas cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells (Figure 2E–G; green cells, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data after regressing out cell cycle genes, and supported by prior lineage tracing data.

claims.claim: Cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells.
claims.source: Thus, cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells (Figure 2E–G; support cells, red), whereas cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells (Figure 2E–G; green cells, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data after regressing out cell cycle genes, and supported by prior lineage tracing data.

claims.claim: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles.
claims.source: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles (Figure 2H), however, 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2H, I.

claims.claim: 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles.
claims.source: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles (Figure 2H), however, 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Cells in the A/P poles and central cells beneath the hair cells are relatively quiescent during homeostasis.
claims.source: Thus, cells in the A/P poles and central cells beneath the hair cells are relatively quiescent during homeostasis (Cruz et al., 2015; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The zona pellucida-like domain-containing protein one gene si:ch73-261i21.5 is expressed in quiescent cells in the A/P poles.
claims.source: The expression of the zona pellucida-like domain-containing protein one gene si:ch73-261i21.5 in the A/P poles has a striking complementary expression pattern to the D/V maker wnt2 and is expressed in quiescent cells (Figure 2J–K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claims.claim: SoxB1 family member sox2, its target sox21a and sox3 are expressed in support and mantle cells but are downregulated in differentiated hair cells.
claims.source: Node 17 shows that the SoxB1 family member sox2, its target sox21a and sox3 are expressed in support and mantle cells but are downregulated in differentiated hair cells (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 8, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary files.

claims.claim: Mantle and all support cells constitute the prosensory domain in a lateral line neuromast.
claims.source: Thus, mantle and all support cells constitute the prosensory domain in a lateral line neuromast.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression of SoxB1 genes in these cells, which characterize the prosensory domain in other species.

claims.claim: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage.
claims.source: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage, whereas clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage (Figure 3B–C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claims.claim: Clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage.
claims.source: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage, whereas clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage (Figure 3B–C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claims.claim: Lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells.
claims.source: Indeed, lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015), whereas mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lineage tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells.
claims.source: Indeed, lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015), whereas mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior lineage tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Quiescent neural stem cells show low levels of ribosomal subunits and protein synthesis.
claims.source: Quiescent neural stem cells show low levels of ribosomal subunits and protein synthesis (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Mantle cells and A/P cells express low levels of rpl and rps genes but these levels significantly increase in clusters 12 and 11 and the dividing cells in clusters 10 and 3.
claims.source: Likewise, we observed mantle (clusters 5, 6) and A/P cells (cluster 13) expressing low levels of rpl (ribosomal protein-L) and rps (ribosomal protein small subunit) genes but these levels significantly increase in clusters 12 and 11 and the dividing cells in clusters 10 and 3 (Figure 3B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The hair cell lineage and the central cells show little ribosome synthesis, which drastically increases in dividing hair cell progenitors.
claims.source: Also, the hair cell lineage and the central cells (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) show little ribosome synthesis, which drastically increases in dividing hair cell progenitors (Figure 3C', Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3C' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Central support and mantle cells resemble quiescent stem or progenitor cells based on their low ribosome synthesis levels.
claims.source: The low ribosome synthesis levels suggest that central support and mantle cells resemble quiescent stem or progenitor cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ribosome synthesis data and comparison to quiescent stem cells in other systems.

claims.claim: When sost+ cells are displaced towards the center of the neuromasts, they downregulate sost and differentiate into hair cells.
claims.source: However, when sost+ cells are displaced towards the center of the neuromasts, they downregulate sost and differentiate into hair cells (lineage from clusters 11/14 to 4, green arrow in Figure 3B and G).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data and supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3B and G.

claims.claim: The differentiating lineage is marked by atoh1a which specifies hair cells together with the downstream delta ligands.
claims.source: The differentiating lineage is marked by atoh1a which specifies hair cells together with the downstream delta ligands (Figures 3H and 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 3H and 4A.

claims.claim: atoh1a is expressed in non-cycling (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) and cycling hair cell progenitors (cluster 4), as well as young hair cells (cluster 2).
claims.source: atoh1a is expressed in non-cycling (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) and cycling hair cell progenitors (cluster 4), as well as young hair cells (cluster 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Central cells are marked by progenitor markers slc1a3a/glasta, lfng, ebf3a, gata2b and prox1a.
claims.source: These cells belong to a subset of central support cells that are marked by progenitor markers slc1a3a/glasta, lfng, ebf3a, gata2b and prox1a (Figure 1I–J and Figure 3I–K, Supplementary file 8, nodes 26, 22 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 1I-J and 3I-K.

claims.claim: Time lapse analyses of regenerating neuromasts in a prox1a reporter line show that central cells downregulate prox1a as they divide, while turning on the hair cell marker pou4f3:gfp.
claims.source: Indeed, time lapse analyses of regenerating neuromasts in a prox1a reporter line show that central cells downregulate prox1a as they divide, while turning on the hair cell marker pou4f3:gfp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3-video 1), as described for the mouse cochlea (Bermingham-McDonogh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and a citation to prior research in the mouse cochlea.

claims.claim: Central cells (clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4) contain or represent hair cell progenitors.
claims.source: We conclude that central cells (clusters 7, 9, 8,14 and 4) contain or represent hair cell progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns and time-lapse data.

claims.claim: Hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells (cluster 1) based on differential gene expression.
claims.source: However, hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells based on differential gene expression (cluster 1; Supplementary file 3, nodes 1 and 2), but the younger hair cells in cluster two possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin (Figure 1R–S; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and experimental observations shown in Figure 1R-S and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Younger hair cells in cluster 2 possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin.
claims.source: However, hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells based on differential gene expression (cluster 1; Supplementary file 3, nodes 1 and 2), but the younger hair cells in cluster two possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin (Figure 1R–S; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1R-S and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: fndc7a labels support cells and the more apically located young and mature hair cells are unlabeled.
claims.source: For example, in situ hybridization with fndc7a shows that it labels support cells as in the mouse and that the more apically located young and mature hair cells are unlabeled (Figure 4K; Maass et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4K and a citation to prior research in the mouse.

claims.claim: A Tg(NFκB:EGFP) reporter line shows that the NFκB pathway is expressed in support cells but that hair cells are GFP-negative.
claims.source: Likewise, a Tg(NFκB:EGFP) reporter line shows that the NFκB pathway that regulates proliferation and self-renewal in other systems is expressed in support cells but that hair cells are GFP-negative (Figure 4L–N; Kanther et al., 2011; Rinkenbaugh and Baldwin, 2016; Zakaria et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data from the reporter line shown in Figure 4L-N and citations to prior research on NFκB.

claims.claim: Genes associated with regulation of transcription, translation, protein folding, cell cycle and Wnt signaling are downregulated in clusters 1 and 2.
claims.source: A GO term analysis reveals that genes associated with regulation of transcription, translation, protein folding, cell cycle and Wnt signaling are downregulated in clusters 1 and 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Genes associated with translation, regulation of cell cycle and Notch signaling (dla, dlb, dlc, dld) are downregulated as hair cells develop from young to mature hair cells.
claims.source: Another group of genes is downregulated as hair cells develop from young to mature hair cells (Figure 4O, Supplementary file 8, node 2 and 24). These downregulated genes are associated with the GO terms translation, regulation of cell cycle and Notch signaling (dla, dlb, dlc, dld).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 4O and supplementary files.

claims.claim: Fgf pathway genes are downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death.
claims.source: Our previous bulk RNA-Seq analysis of regenerating neuromasts revealed that Fgf pathway genes are downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death ((Jiang et al., 2014; Figure 5A–H') suggesting that the downregulation of Fgf signaling could be involved in triggering regeneration, as was shown for Notch signaling (Ma et al., 2008; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior bulk RNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A-H', and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae.
claims.source: Indeed, hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae and even during homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased (Figure 5I–L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L.

claims.claim: During homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased in fgf3 mutant larvae.
claims.source: Indeed, hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae and even during homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased (Figure 5I–L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L.

claims.claim: fgf3 is expressed exclusively in central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9) and is downregulated in response to death of the overlying hair cells.
claims.source: The scRNA-Seq analysis of homeostatic neuromasts shows that ligand and receptor expression is complex, and that Fgf signaling is not active in young or mature hair cells (Figure 5M; clusters 2, 1). fgf3 is expressed exclusively in central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9) and is downregulated in response to death of the overlying hair cells (Figure 5A').
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5M and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A'.

claims.claim: fgf3 and prox1a are co-expressed in central support cells.
claims.source: We generated a fgf3 knock-in line that recapitulates fgf3 expression (Figure 5N–O, Figure 5-video 1) and a cross with a prox1a reporter line shows that fgf3 and prox1a are co-expressed, as predicted by the scRNA-Seq data (Figure 5P–Q).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data from the fgf3 knock-in and prox1a reporter lines shown in Figure 5P-Q.

claims.claim: During both homeostasis and regeneration, proliferation is significantly increased in fgf3-/- neuromasts.
claims.source: To understand the cellular basis of the increased regeneration response, we performed BrdU analyses of homeostatic and regenerating fgf3-deficient neuromasts. During both homeostasis and regeneration, proliferation is significantly increased in fgf3-/- neuromasts (Figure 6A–F).

results.result: scRNA-Seq analysis of 1521 homeostatic neuromast cells identified seven major cell types including differentiated hair cells (cluster 1), young hair cells (cluster 2), proliferating hair cell progenitors (cluster 4), amplifying support cells (clusters 3, 10), central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9, 14), and mantle cells (clusters 5, 6). These clusters were validated by in situ hybridization of marker genes showing distinct spatial localization patterns within neuromasts.
results.evaluation: The scRNA-Seq clustering analysis (C20-C25) is well-supported by computational methods and validated by in situ hybridization experiments (C26-C29, C36, C39). Cell cycle gene expression patterns (C41-C44) provide additional support for distinguishing proliferating populations. The integration of computational clustering with spatial validation provides strong converging evidence for the identified cell types.

results.result: Proliferating support cells were spatially compartmentalized: cluster 3 cells represent amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells in D/V poles (6.5% proliferation rate), while cluster 4 cells are central support cells that differentiate into hair cells. A/P pole cells and central cells are relatively quiescent during homeostasis (0-1% proliferation).
results.evaluation: The spatial compartmentalization of proliferating cells is supported by BrdU labeling data (C47-C48), regression analysis of cell cycle genes (C45-C46), and in situ hybridization of spatial markers (C50). The integration of scRNA-Seq clustering with prior lineage tracing data strengthens these conclusions.

results.result: Two distinct cell lineages were identified: an amplifying lineage (clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10, 3) expressing sox2/sox21a/sox3 and showing low ribosomal gene expression in quiescent states, and a differentiating hair cell lineage (clusters 7, 9, 8, 14, 4) with increased ribosome synthesis upon activation. Mantle and support cells constitute the prosensory domain.
results.evaluation: The lineage assignments are supported by hierarchical clustering analysis (C53-C54), gene expression patterns (C51, C58-C59), and validated by prior lineage tracing experiments (C55-C56). The ribosomal gene expression patterns (C58-C60) provide additional molecular evidence consistent with quiescent versus activated stem cell states described in other systems.

results.result: Pseudotime analysis ordered cells along a developmental trajectory from central support cells (clusters 7, 9, 8, 14) expressing progenitor markers (slc1a3a/glasta, lfng, ebf3a, gata2b, prox1a) through proliferating progenitors (cluster 4) expressing atoh1a to young (cluster 2) and mature hair cells (cluster 1), with progressive downregulation of support cell genes and upregulation of hair cell-specific genes.
results.evaluation: The pseudotime trajectory is supported by PAGA analysis (C4), marker gene expression patterns (C62-C64, C67, C69-C70), time-lapse imaging showing prox1a downregulation during differentiation (C65), and GO term analysis of downregulated genes (C71-C72). The convergence of computational trajectory inference with experimental validation provides strong support.

results.result: Loss of fgf3, which is expressed exclusively in central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9) and downregulated after hair cell death, leads to significantly increased proliferation during both homeostasis and regeneration, with amplifying divisions no longer restricted to D/V poles. Similar phenotypes were observed with fgfr1a/fgfr2 double mutants and dn:fgfr1a expression.
results.evaluation: The role of fgf3 in inhibiting proliferation is supported by scRNA-Seq localization data (C76), fgf3 knock-in reporter validation (C77), BrdU proliferation assays in mutants (C78, C82), and genetic validation with receptor mutants (C79-C81). The spatial redistribution of proliferation in mutants (C82) provides additional mechanistic insight.

results.result: scRNA-Seq analysis of fgf3 mutants revealed that fgf3 inhibits proliferation by suppressing Wnt signaling, likely via the Wnt inhibitor sost. In fgf3-/- neuromasts, sost is downregulated, the Wnt target gene wnt10a is upregulated, and Wnt inhibition by dkk1 rescues the increased proliferation phenotype.
results.evaluation: The mechanism is supported by differential gene expression analysis (C86, C117), in situ validation of sost downregulation (C87-C88), upregulation of Wnt target genes (C89), and genetic epistasis experiments showing dkk1 rescues the fgf3 mutant phenotype (C90). The convergence of expression data with functional rescue experiments provides strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Epistasis experiments demonstrate that Notch and Fgf signaling act largely in parallel to inhibit Wnt signaling and proliferation. Notch pathway genes are unaffected in fgf3-/- mutants, and NICD activation inhibits proliferation in both wildtype and fgf3-/- backgrounds, though Notch may play a minor role in maintaining fgf3 expression.
results.evaluation: The parallel pathway model is supported by in situ hybridization showing no effect of fgf3 loss on Notch pathway genes (C92), slight downregulation of fgf3 after Notch inhibition (C93-C94), and crucially, NICD overexpression experiments showing Notch can inhibit proliferation independently of Fgf3 (C95-C97). The epistasis experiments provide strong evidence for parallel rather than linear pathway architecture.

results.result: The authors propose that neuromasts contain both active stem cells (amplifying cells in D/V poles that self-renew continuously) and quiescent stem cells (A/P compartment cells and mantle cells), with cell fate determined by location and signals rather than predetermined lineages. Support cells can convert to mantle cells when mantle cells are ablated.
results.evaluation: The stem cell model is supported by PAGA connectivity analysis showing transitions between lineages (C100), proliferation patterns (C47-C49, C102-C103), and citations to prior lineage tracing studies (C104-C105). However, the quiescent stem cell designation for A/P cells (C103) is more speculative as it requires long-term lineage tracing validation that is acknowledged as future work.

results.result: Support cells express genes characteristic of stem cells in other organs including slc1a3a/glasta and prominin1a/b (neural stem cell markers), hopx and alpl (intestinal/hair follicle stem cell markers), and fabp7/Blbp and isl1 (neural and cardiac stem cell markers), suggesting conserved stem cell programs across tissues.
results.evaluation: The conservation of stem cell markers is supported by scRNA-Seq expression data (C110-C111) and multiple citations to prior research establishing these genes as stem cell markers in other systems (C109, C112-C113). However, the functional significance of this expression pattern in neuromasts requires experimental validation beyond expression correlation.

results.result: Ribosomal protein gene expression analysis revealed that mantle cells, A/P cells, and central support cells show low ribosome synthesis characteristic of quiescent stem cells, while activated/dividing cells show increased ribosomal gene expression, consistent with stem cell activation patterns in other systems.
results.evaluation: The ribosomal gene expression patterns (C58-C59) are well-documented in the scRNA-Seq data and the interpretation is supported by multiple citations to prior research on quiescent stem cells in other systems (C57, C106-C107). The inference that low ribosome synthesis indicates quiescence (C60) is reasonable but correlative rather than causative.

results.result: The inhibitory effect of Fgf signaling on proliferation appears evolutionarily conserved, as Wnt signaling induces proliferation in mammalian hair cell progenitors, Fgf inhibits proliferation in chicken utricle and basilar papilla, and Fgf2/Fgf20 inhibit support cell proliferation in mammalian cultures. Sostdc1 may be the relevant Wnt inhibitor in mammals.
results.evaluation: The evolutionary conservation is supported by multiple citations to prior research in mammals and birds (C118, C122-C123), database evidence for Sostdc1 expression in mammalian ear (C119), and the authors' data in zebrafish. However, the specific mechanism via Sostdc1 in mammals (C119) requires experimental validation. The speculation about alternative mechanisms via Sprouty2 (C120-C121) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: While fgf3's main role appears to be regulating proliferation, it may also maintain hair cell progenitors in an undifferentiated state, though this effect is subtle as only limited increases in hair cell numbers are observed and scRNA-Seq did not reveal obvious cell fate regulators.
results.evaluation: This claim is appropriately presented as speculation (C125) based on analogy to developing zebrafish ear and mouse cochlea studies (C126-C127). The authors acknowledge the effect would be subtle (C128) and that their scRNA-Seq analysis did not identify clear candidates for fate regulation. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future investigation rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: The authors propose that in mammals, short-term inhibition of Notch and/or Fgf pathways may be more effective for functional regeneration than prolonged treatments, based on observations that both pathways are reactivated before regeneration is complete in zebrafish.
results.evaluation: This is presented as speculation (C131) for mammalian therapy based on zebrafish observations. While the parallel inhibition of Wnt by both pathways is well-supported in zebrafish (C130), the translation to optimal mammalian treatment strategies requires experimental validation. The temporal dynamics argument is logical but not directly tested.

results.result: Background context establishing that hair cell loss causes deafness in mammals but regenerates in non-mammalian vertebrates, the zebrafish lateral line is a valid model system with evolutionarily conserved hair cell structure and function, and prior work identified two major support cell lineages (amplifying and differentiating) with spatial compartmentalization.
results.evaluation: These background claims are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature (C1-C2, C6-C15) and the authors' own prior work (C16-C19). This establishes the scientific context and rationale for the current study. All claims are appropriately referenced and represent established knowledge in the field.
